title: The Cancellation Climb

scenario.situation: Rider cancellations rose 30% the month surge pricing was tweaked.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The pricing PM is convinced the surge change caused riders to bail and wants it reverted city-wide immediately.
scenario.question: Is the surge tweak actually driving cancellations — and if so, where?

decisions.prompt: The PM wants an answer fast. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Before/after analysis on the surge change date
options.detail: Compare total cancellation rates in the weeks before and after the surge tweak shipped.
options.consequence: Cancellations did rise after the date — but so did the start of peak-season demand. The timing is consistent with the PM's story, yet it can't separate surge from any other concurrent change. You've confirmed a timeline, not a cause.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the PM's narrative and conflated timing with causation.

options.label: Diagnostic segmentation by zone and time-of-day
options.detail: Break cancellations down by geographic zone, hour block, and whether surge was active to see where the increase actually concentrates.
options.consequence: The segmentation immediately shows the 30% lift is not uniform across the city — it clusters sharply in specific zones at specific hours. This opens a thread the price hypothesis alone never would have.

options.label: Regression of surge multiplier against cancellation rate
options.detail: Model cancellation rate as a function of the surge multiplier across all rides.
options.consequence: The city-wide regression returns a modest positive coefficient on surge — plausible but weak. Aggregating across zones with very different supply conditions buries the real signal in noise.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to city-wide modeling that averaged away the localized driver.

options.label: Pull rider complaints and support tickets
options.detail: Scan cancellation-related support contacts to understand what riders are saying.
options.consequence: Tickets mention long wait times and high prices — both — but the sample skews toward the angriest riders and can't tell you whether the root cause is supply or price. Useful color, not a diagnosis.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a biased, anecdotal signal when structured data could answer the question directly.

decisions.prompt: Segmenting by zone reveals some zones look very different. Which metric do you use to confirm the pattern?

artifact.title: Raw cancellation counts by zone — current month
artifact.caption: Raw cancelled ride counts. Outer zones look high — but are they actually riskier, or just busier this month?

options.label: Raw cancellation counts by zone
options.detail: Compare the absolute number of cancellations across zones.
options.consequence: Outer East and Outer West do show big counts — but request volume also spiked in those zones this month. You're reading demand growth, not necessarily a worse cancellation problem. The signal is confounded by zone size.
options.divergenceCost: Compared absolute counts across zones with different request volumes — read size, not risk.

options.label: Cancellation rate by zone × peak-hour block (normalized)
options.detail: Cancellations as a percentage of ride requests, split by zone and hour block.
options.consequence: Normalized and sliced by time, the picture is unmistakable: Outer East and Outer West spike to 38–41% cancellation rates during peak hours — versus 7–9% citywide. Downtown and Midtown are flat. The surge tweak zones are unremarkable; supply collapse at peak hours in the outer zones is the real signal.

artifact.title: Peak-hour cancellation RATE by zone (% of requests cancelled)
artifact.caption: Normalized to requests per zone, the outer zones dwarf the rest at peak hours. Surge-affected zones are unremarkable.

decisions.prompt: Outer-zone peak-hour cancellation rates are 4–5× the city average, and driver supply data shows a sharp drop in those zones at those hours. What do you tell the PM?

options.label: "It's a supply collapse in the outer zones — don't revert surge, fix driver incentives there."
options.detail: Make the causal call and prescribe the fix directly.
options.consequence: You've given the PM a confident, action-ready answer — but you've leapt from correlation to cause. If an unobserved factor (e.g., a competing platform's promotion pulling drivers away) is driving both low supply and high cancellations, the prescribed fix still misses it. Confidence without a causal check risks a costly misdirection.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation from correlational zone-level data.

options.label: "The 30% lift concentrates in two outer zones at peak hours — not citywide. Supply, not price, is the stronger correlate. A city-wide revert would leave the real problem untouched. Recommend a targeted driver-incentive pilot in those zones to confirm the supply hypothesis before any pricing change."
options.detail: Report the finding, flag the causal gap, and propose a targeted test.
options.consequence: You've reframed the PM's city-wide narrative with granular evidence, stayed honest about what correlation can and can't prove, and handed leadership a cheap, targeted test that will confirm or refute the supply story before committing to any policy change.

insight: The 30% cancellation rise wasn't a pricing story — it was a supply story hidden inside a city-wide average. Two outer zones at peak hours accounted for almost all the lift; every other zone was flat. The trap was a plausible narrative (something changed, blame that thing) and a metric — raw city-wide cancellations — that was technically correct but analytically useless at the aggregate level. The lesson: before attributing a city-wide metric shift to the one thing that changed, segment by the dimensions that could reveal where the shift actually lives.
